## Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) {#sec-utc .hiddenheading}

There are 12 [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offsets that become a [terminating decimals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repeating_decimal#:~:text=a%20finite%20number%20of%20nonzero%20digits) in [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"} after being converted from hours to days and therefore could be displayed in either [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"} or [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"}. Although it has only ten time zones, Dec can match the time in any [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} time zone with one or two non-negative [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} digits. There are 27 UTC offsets that require only one [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} digit and 11 that need two [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} digits.

Out of the [38](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_UTC_offsets) [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offsets, 14 are negative (&lt;[UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"}) and 24 are non-negative (&ge;[UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"}). The [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} time zone with [the most negative offset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC%E2%88%9212:00#:~:text=a%20nautical%20time%20zone%20comprising%20the%20high%20seas%20between%20180%C2%B0%20and%20172%C2%B030%E2%80%B2W%20longitude) is completely uninhabited. The bar chart below visualizes [Socioeconomic Data and Applications Center](https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/centers/sedac-daac) data from 2020 regarding the population of each [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} time zone. The vast majority of all people live in [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} time zones with &ge;[UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offsets.

{{< include /dec/time/_tzpopplot.qmd >}}

Negative [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offsets only exist in [the Americas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americas#:~:text=a%20landmass%20comprising%20the%20totality%20of%20North%20America%20and%20South%20America) and islands in the [Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_islands_in_the_Atlantic_Ocean) and [Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_islands_in_the_Pacific_Ocean) Oceans. Therefore, the bar chart above is essentially comparing the populations of the Americas and the rest of the world. According to 2021 [United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Department_of_Economic_and_Social_Affairs#:~:text=part%20of%20the%20United%20Nations%20Secretariat) data, roughly 1 billion out of a total of almost 8 billion people live in the Americas.

Dec forbids the association of dates with negative offsets. Therefore, Dec will add ten [decidays]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenths of a day"} to any negative offset and add one day to the date associated with that offset. Negative offset handling has no effect on the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} or the conversion of an [hms](#hms){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour minute second"} triplet to a [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} and is typically only necessary after a "year month day" ([ymd](#ymd){#yearmonthday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year month day"}) triplet is converted into a Dec date.

If we do know whether Day [364]{.color364by365} belongs to a common or leap year, adding one day to it yields either Day [0]{.color0} or Day [365]{.color365by366} and this uncertainty is expressed as a [multiplication sign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiplication_sign) over the last digit of [36[5]{.acutegrave}]{.color0}. The sign hints that [36[5]{.acutegrave}]{.color0} is short for [365]{.color0}&times;`leap`, where [36[5]{.acutegrave}]{.color0} is either [365]{.color365by366} if `leap` is 1 or [0]{.color0} if `leap` is 0. We can find `leap` by passing any year ([y](#y){#year .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year"}) to @eq-leap below.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup07}
$$
\text{leap}=\begin{cases}
  1&{\begin{aligned}
    &\text{ if } (\text{y} + 1)\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder%20or%20signed%20remainder%20of%20a%20division}{\bmod} \ \ \ \ 4=0\\
    &\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_conjunction}{\land}(\text{y} + 1)\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder%20or%20signed%20remainder%20of%20a%20division}{\bmod} 100\neq0\\
    &\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_disjunction}{\lor}(\text{y} + 1)\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder%20or%20signed%20remainder%20of%20a%20division}{\bmod} 400=0\end{aligned}}\\\\
  0&{\text{ otherwise}}\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-leap}

:::

# Day of week {#sec-dow .hiddenheading}

Adding one day to the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} has no effect on the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}, but it increments the [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of month"} and "day of week" ([dow](#dow){#dayofweek .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"}). Dec meets the expectations of [Gregorian calendar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregorian_calendar#:~:text=the%20calendar%20currently%20used%20in%20most%20parts%20of%20the%20world) users who live in [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} time zones with negative offsets by essentially deriving the previous [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of month"} or [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of week"} from the current [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} if a location in the Americas is provided without an offset or with a negative offset.

# Time zone offset {#sec-tzo .hiddenheading}

In Dec, "time zone offsets" ([tzo](#tzo){#timezoneoffset .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offsets"}) are derived solely from longitude. Dec measures [longitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longitude#:~:text=denoted%20by%20the%20Greek%20letter%20lambda) in [wěi](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E7%B7%AF#:~:text=(geography)-,latitude,-coordinate%20terms%C2%A0%E2%96%B2) ([w](#w){#wei .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="horizontal lines on a map"}), arcbeats ([a](#a){#arcbeat .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="arcbeats"}), or submultiples thereof. If we travel East or West until we reach our starting point, we will cover 1 [w](#w){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="horizontal line on a map"} or 100000 ([10^5^]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="a hundred thousand"}) [a](#a){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="arcbeats"}. A [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offsets"} is essentially a [deciwěi]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenth of a wěi"} ([dw](#dw){#deciwei .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="deciwěi"}) longitude that became a single-digit [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"} integer via  [truncation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truncation#Truncation_and_floor_function:~:text=truncation%20is%20limiting%20the%20number%20of%20digits%20right%20of%20the%20decimal%20point) or [flooring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floor_and_ceiling_functions#:~:text=takes%20as%20input%20a%20real%20number%20x%2C%20and%20gives%20as%20output%20the%20greatest%20integer%20less%20than%20or%20equal%20to%20x): &LeftFloor;\${longInputHsl} &div; 100&RightFloor; = \${longFloorHsl}.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: loninput
//| class: slider
viewof lonInput = Inputs.range([0, 999], {label: "Milliwěi", value: 500, step: 1})
```

The [Equator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equator#:~:text=the%20circle%20of%20latitude%20that%20divides%20Earth%20into%20the%20Northern%20and%20Southern%20Hemispheres) is approximately ([~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}) 1 [taur]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="circumference = 𝜏r"} ([c](#c){#taur .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="taur"}) or [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}[10^5^]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="a hundred thousand"} [kilozem]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousands of zone equatorial meters"} ([kz](#kz){#kilozem .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousands of zone equatorial meters"}) long. Near the Equator, a longitude that has a [precision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decimal_degrees#Precision) of 0.1 [microwěi]{#microwei .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millionths of wěi"} ([&micro;w](#uw){#microwei .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="microwěi"}) or 10 milliarcbeats ([ma](#ma){#milliarcbeats .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliarcbeats"}) is accurate to within [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}0.1 [microtaur]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millionths of taur"} ([&micro;c](#uc){#microtaur .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="microtaur"}), [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}10 "zone equatorial meters" ([zem]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="zone equatorial meters"}), or 4 [meters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metre#Definition:~:text=the%20base%20unit%20of%20length%20in%20the%20International%20System%20of%20Units), which is about the width of a [U-shaped living room layout](https://www.dimensions.com/collection/living-room-layouts) or the length of a typical [subcompact car](https://www.dimensions.com/collection/subcompact-cars-b-segment).

For precise [geopositioning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geopositioning#:~:text=estimating%20the%20geographic%20position%20of%20an%20object%20or%20a%20person), we may want to express [geographic coordinates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geographic_coordinate_system#:~:text=for%20measuring%20and%20communicating%20positions%20directly%20on%20Earth%20as%20latitude%20and%20longitude) in [ma](#ma){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliarcbeats"}, but we are unlikely to need [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"} or [cmd](#cmd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="centimillidays"} when displaying the [solar time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_time#:~:text=a%20calculation%20of%20the%20passage%20of%20time%20based%20on%20the%20position%20of%20the%20Sun%20in%20the%20sky) or estimates of what the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} will be when the Sun rises, reaches its [highest point of the day](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noon#:~:text=highest%20position%20above%20the%20horizon), or sets. By default, Dec uses [md](#md){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millidays"} precision to display a solar time and the "solar time offset" ([sto](#sto){#solartimeoffset .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar time offset"}) used to produce it.

# Solar time offset {#sec-sto .hiddenheading}

Dec never forces anyone to change their offset and therefore has nothing like [daylight saving time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daylight_saving_time). In Dec, any offset can be referred to as a [sto](#sto){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar time offset"}, even if it is not used to match solar time, but there are only 10 [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offsets"}, because there are only 10 Dec time zones. Dec translates [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} to Zone [0]{.color0} and UTC[-]{.mono}12:00 or UTC+12:00 to Zone [5]{.color5}, but all other [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offsets are considered [sto](#sto){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar time offsets"} and not [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offsets"}.

Anyone can use any offset at any time, as long as they provide the offset after the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}. A Dec time is [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}[-]{.mono}offset, just like a [Dec date](/dec/date) is year+day. For example, when I wrote this paragraph, my Dec date was 2026+242 and my Dec time was .520[-]{.mono}[8]{.color8}. Like Dec dates, Dec times are truncated math expressions. When we evaluate the expression represented by a Dec time, we get a Zone [0]{.color0} [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}, as shown in @eq-zone0tod. Unlike a [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}, which can be written without a dot in the unit of its last digit, an offset never has a dot but is always read as if it were preceded by one, so its first digit is in [dd](#dd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="decidays"}. The offset [8]{.color8} is 0.8 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"}, and 700[-]{.mono}[8]{.color8} is the same time as 900[-]{.mono}[0]{.color0}. If my current time is .520[-]{.mono}[8]{.color8}, the time in Zone [0]{.color0} is .720[-]{.mono}[0]{.color0}: (.520 [-]{.mono} 0.8) mod 1 = .720.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup08}
$$\text{zone0tod} = (\text{tod} - .\text{offset}) \bmod 1$$ {#eq-zone0tod}
:::

The default offset is like a user preference that Dec can remember and update as needed. If a user does not select a default offset, Dec will try to infer their default offset from their longitude, and if offset inference fails, the final fallback is a default offset of [0]{.color0}. If someone wants to change their default offset for a certain period of time, Dec supports automatic offset changes based on user instructions. Users can share automatic offset changes, but they have to opt in to any change to their default offset instead of opting out of a required change. The [Dec span](/dec/span) article will describe automatic offset changes in more detail.

A default offset can have up to six digits that mix [b9](#b9){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base9"}, [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"}, and [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} as desired. This flexibility is meant to support scientific and technical purposes, so users are advised to choose one of the ten [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offsets"}, which requires only one [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"} digit. Dec may simplify the selected default offset. For example, [α]{.color0} and [☉]{.color0} are the same as [0]{.color0}, and there is not much point in displaying [α]{.color0} or [☉]{.color0} when [0]{.color0} is easier to understand. Dec stores the default offset as both a string and a decimal number. The string is displayed to the user and the decimal number is used to adjust the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}. Swatch Internet Time, for instance, would be displayed as [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}[-]{.mono}[β]{.color1by24}, because its time zone is 1 hour or 1/24 of a day ahead of Zone [0]{.color0}.

China is a good example of the difference between a [sto](#sto){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar time offset"} and a [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offset"}. The territory of China spans three Dec time zones, Zones [2]{.color2}, [3]{.color3}, and [4]{.color4}, but the government of China has decided that everyone in China should use UTC+08:00, which is Earth ([♁]{.color3by9}) in [b9](#b9){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base9"} or iota ([ι]{.color8by24}) in [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"}. Dec does not enforce the use of any offset, but it would suggest that users in China consider a [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offset"} of [3]{.color3} [dd](#dd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="decidays"}, which is not far off from 8/24, 1/3, [♁]{.color3by9}, or [ι]{.color8by24}. Zone [3]{.color3} may actually be closer to the [sto](#sto){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar time offset"} of most people in China, because the center of Zone [3]{.color3}, 350 [mw](#mw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliwěi"}, is close to the geographic center of China, [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}337 [mw](#mw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliwěi"}, whereas the central longitude of UTC+08:00, [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}383 [mw](#mw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliwěi"}, is much further East.

To get a local solar time, we add a [sto](#sto){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar time offset"} to a Zone [0]{.color0} [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}. If the [sto](#sto){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar time offset"} accounts only for longitude, the result is an [mst](#mst){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mean solar time"}. If it also includes the [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"}, the result is an [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"}. Whereas a Dec time zone spans a [dw](#dw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="deciwěi"}, a [sto](#sto){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar time offset"} represents a single longitude. In @eq-mst below, the [sto](#sto){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar time offset"} of a longitude in [w](#w){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="horizontal lines on a map"} is (0.95 + [w](#w){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="horizontal lines on a map"}) mod 1.

# Equation of time {#sec-eot .hiddenheading}

The two types of [solar time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_time#:~:text=a%20calculation%20of%20the%20passage%20of%20time%20based%20on%20the%20position%20of%20the%20Sun%20in%20the%20sky) are ["mean solar time"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_time#Mean_solar_time:~:text=it%20follows%20an%20imaginary%20%22mean%20Sun%22%20that%20moves%20along%20the%20celestial%20equator%20at%20a%20constant%20rate%20that%20matches%20the%20real%20Sun%27s%20average%20rate%20over%20the%20year) ([mst](#mst){#meansolartime .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mean solar time"}) and ["apparent solar time"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_time#Apparent_solar_time:~:text=the%20apparent%20motion%20of%20the%20actual%20Sun) ([ast](#ast){#apparentsolartime .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"}). To calculate an [mst](#mst){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mean solar time"}, we keep only the decimal part of the sum of 0.95, the Zone [0]{.color0} [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} measured in days, and a longitude measured in [w](#w){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="horizontal lines on a map"}. If we want [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"} instead of [mst](#mst){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mean solar time"}, the sum needs to include the result of plugging the "time of year" ([toy](#toy){#timeofyear .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of year"}) into the ["equation of time"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equation_of_time#:~:text=the%20discrepancy%20between%20two%20kinds%20of%20solar%20time) ([eot](#eot){#equationoftime .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"}).

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup09}
$$\text{syl} = \text{leap} + 365$$ {#eq-syl}

$$\text{toy} = \text{ada} \div \text{syl}$$ {#eq-toy}

$$\text{mst} = (0.95 + \text{tod} + \text{w}) \bmod 1$$ {#eq-mst}

$$\text{ast} = (0.95 + \text{tod} + \text{w} +  \text{eot}) \bmod 1$$ {#eq-ast}
:::

To obtain a [toy](#toy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of year"}, we divide an [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"} by a "solar year length" ([syl](#syl){#solaryearlength .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar year length"}), which is the number of days in the year. Dec passes the [toy](#toy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of year"} directly from @eq-toy to the [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} function in @eq-eot without first multiplying it by 2𝜋 or 𝜏 to convert it from [turns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turn_%28angle%29#:~:text=a%20unit%20of%20plane%20angle%20measurement%20equal%20to%202%CF%80%C2%A0radians%2C%20360%C2%A0degrees) ([t](#t){#turn .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"}) to [radians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radian#:~:text=the%20unit%20of%20angle%20in%20the%20International%20System%20of%20Units) ([rad](#rad){#radian .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="radians"}) because the [sin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sine_and_cosine#:~:text=the%20ratio%20of%20the%20length%20of%20the%20side%20opposite%20that%20angle%20to%20the%20length%20of%20the%20longest%20side%20of%20the%20triangle) and [cos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sine_and_cosine#:~:text=the%20ratio%20of%20the%20length%20of%20the%20adjacent%20leg%20to%20that%20of%20the%20hypotenuse) [trigonometric functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigonometric_functions#:~:text=functions%20which%20relate%20an%20angle%20of%20a%20right%2Dangled%20triangle%20to%20ratios%20of%20two%20side%20lengths) used by Dec are designed for [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"} instead of [rad](#rad){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="radians"}.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup10}
$$\begin{split}
\text{eot} & = \beta_0 \\
& + \beta_1 \ast \text{cos(toy)} \\
& + \beta_2 \ast \text{sin(toy)} \\
& + \beta_3 \ast \text{cos(2} \ast \text{toy)} \\
& + \beta_4 \ast \text{sin(2} \ast \text{toy)}
\end{split}$$ {#eq-eot}
:::

By comparing the `sincost` and `sincos` functions, the code below demonstrates that using [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"} rather than [rad](#rad){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="radians"} can [yield more accurate results](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sine_and_cosine#:~:text=Representing%20angles%20in%20turns%20or%20half%2Dturns%20has%20accuracy%20advantages). Whereas `sincost` expects to receive [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"} and is always correct, `sincos` assumes that it will get [rad](#rad){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="radians"} and generates the slightly incorrect [E notation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_notation#E_notation) values below because it cannot produce zero unless its input is zero.

:::{.panel-tabset group="language"}
### Julia

```{julia}
sincost(x) = sincospi(2 * x)
sincost(0.25)
sincost(0.5)
sincost(0.75)
sincost(1)
sincos(0.25 * 2 * pi)
sincos(0.5 * 2 * pi)
sincos(0.75 * 2 * pi)
sincos(1 * 2 * pi)
```

### Observable JavaScript

```{ojs}
sincospi = require(
  'https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/stdlib-js/math-base-special-sincospi@umd/browser.js'
  )
function sincost(x) {
  return sincospi(2 * x);
}
function sincos(x) {
  return [Math.sin(x), Math.cos(x)]
}
sincost(0.25)
sincost(0.5)
sincost(0.75)
sincost(1)
sincos(0.25 * 2 * Math.PI)
sincos(0.5 * 2 * Math.PI)
sincos(0.75 * 2 * Math.PI)
sincos(1 * 2 * Math.PI)
```

### Python

```{python}
from math import cos, sin, pi, cospi, sinpi

def sincost(x):
    x *= 2
    return sinpi(x), cospi(x)

def sincos(x):
    return sin(x), cos(x)

sincost(0.25)
sincost(0.5)
sincost(0.75)
sincost(1)
sincos(0.25 * 2 * pi)
sincos(0.5 * 2 * pi)
sincos(0.75 * 2 * pi)
sincos(1 * 2 * pi)
```

### R

```{r}
sincost <- function(x) {
  x <- 2 * x
  c(sinpi(x), cospi(x))
}

sincos <- function(x) {
  c(sin(x), cos(x))
}

sincost(0.25)
sincost(0.5)
sincost(0.75)
sincost(1)
sincos(0.25 * 2 * pi)
sincos(0.5 * 2 * pi)
sincos(0.75 * 2 * pi)
sincos(1 * 2 * pi)
```

:::

The values below are the coefficients of a [harmonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic#:~:text=positive%20integer%20multiple%20of%20the%20fundamental%20frequency) [model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_model#:~:text=embodies%20a%20set%20of%20statistical%20assumptions%20concerning%20the%20generation%20of%20sample%20data), adapted from the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration](https://www.noaa.gov) ([NOAA](#noaa){#nationaloceanicandatmosphericadministration .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration"}) [General Solar Position Calculations](https://gml.noaa.gov/grad/solcalc/solareqns.PDF). Before [fitting](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.optimize.curve_fit.html) the model to [NOAA](#noaa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration"} [yearly solar data](https://gml.noaa.gov/grad/solcalc/calcdetails.html), Dec divides [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} values by 1.44 to convert minutes to [md](#md){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millidays"}, converts [ymd](#ymd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year month day"} triplet dates and [hms](#hms){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour minute second"} triplet times into [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregates"}, and sorts by [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"}.

{{< embed eot.ipynb#eotcoef >}}

{{< include /dec/time/_eotplot.qmd >}}

In the [line📈chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_chart#:~:text=a%20type%20of%20chart%20that%20displays%20information%20as%20a%20series%20of%20data%20points%20called%20%27markers%27%20connected%20by%20straight%20line%20segments) above, the [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} values range from -9.8 to 11.4 [md](#md){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millidays"} and the range of [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of year"}, [-365]{.color0} to [365]{.color365by366}, represents a common year followed by a leap year. The [absolute value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_value#:~:text=non%2Dnegative%29-,magnitude%20of,measured%20without%20regard%20to%20its%20sign,-.%20Namely%2C) of the [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} reaches about one [centiday]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hundredth of a day"} ([cd]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="centiday"}) on Days [245]{.color245by365} and [349]{.color349by365}, but passes through zero on Days [45]{.color045by365}, [103]{.color103by365}, [184]{.color184by365}, and [299]{.color299by365}. Therefore, [mst](#mst){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mean solar time"} and [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"} are equivalent four times per year.

Apart from transforming an [mst](#mst){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mean solar time"} into an [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"}, we can also use [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} values to more accurately estimate the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="times of day"} of [solar noon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noon#:~:text=reaching%20its%20highest%20position%20above%20the%20horizon%20on%20that%20day%20and%20casting%20the%20shortest%20shadow), sunrise, and sunset. @eq-solarnoon below creates a [solar noon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noon#:~:text=reaching%20its%20highest%20position%20above%20the%20horizon%20on%20that%20day%20and%20casting%20the%20shortest%20shadow) [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} by keeping only the decimal part of the result of subtracting a [w](#w){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="horizontal lines on a map"} longitude and an [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} value that is measured in days from the sum of 9.55 and a [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offset"} that is measured in days.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup11}
$$\text{solarnoon} = \left(9.55 + \text{tzo} - \text{w} - \text{eot}\right) \bmod 1$$ {#eq-solarnoon}
:::

# Cambridge and Cambridge {#sec-cac .hiddenheading}

To compare the solar noon [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} in two cities, we can plug the longitude of each city into @eq-solarnoon above. If all of the variables other than longitude in @eq-solarnoon are set to zero, the resulting solar noon [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} is almost five [decidays]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenths of a day"} for [Cambridge, England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge#:~:text=a%20city%20and%20non%2Dmetropolitan%20district%20in%20the%20county%20of%20Cambridgeshire%2C%20England) in the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom#:~:text=a%20country%20in%20Northwestern%20Europe) and nearly seven [decidays]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenths of a day"} for [Cambridge, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts#:~:text=a%20city%20in%20Middlesex%20County%2C%20Massachusetts%2C%20United%20States) in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States#:~:text=a%20country%20primarily%20located%20in%20North%20America).

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup12}
$$4.99635 = (9.55 - 0.050365) \bmod 1 \ast 10$$ {#eq-cambridgeuk}

$$6.97517 = (9.55 - 0.852484) \bmod 1 \ast 10$$ {#eq-cambridgema}
:::

The two homonymous cities are about two [dw](#dw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="deciwěi"} apart and therefore will always differ by around two [decidays]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenths of a day"} in solar time, regardless of what time zone we use as our frame of reference. England is in Zone [0]{.color0} and Massachusetts is in Zone [8]{.color8}. From the perspective of Zone [8]{.color8}, solar noon is roughly [Tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} [5]{.color5} in Cambridge, MA and about [Tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} [3]{.color3} in Cambridge, UK.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup13}
$$2.99635 = (9.55 + 0.8 - 0.050365) \bmod 1 \ast 10$$ {#eq-cambridgeuk8}

$$4.97517 = (9.55 + 0.8 - 0.852484) \bmod 1 \ast 10$$ {#eq-cambridgema8}
:::

# Light arc whole {#sec-law .hiddenheading}

The path in the sky that the Sun appears to follow from a sunrise to a sunset is a "light [arc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_path#:~:text=arc%2Dlike%20path%20that%20the%20Sun%20appears%20to%20follow%20across%20the%20sky) whole" ([law](#law){#lightarcwhole .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"}). Solar noon, the midpoint of a [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"}, is halfway between sunrise and sunset. A [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} can be evenly split into two "light arc halves" ([lah](#lah){#lightarchalf .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc half"}). Whereas [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="times of day"} are time points, [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc wholes"} and [lah](#lah){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc halves"} are durations. The difference between a solar noon [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} and a [lah](#lah){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc half"} is a sunrise [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup14}
$$\text{law} = \text{lah} \ast 2$$ {#eq-law}

$$\begin{split}
\text{sunrise}
& = \text{solarmidnight} + \text{nah} \\
& = \text{solarnoon} - \text{lah} \\
& = \text{sunset} - \text{law}
\end{split}$$ {#eq-sunrise}

$$\begin{split}
\text{sunset}
& = \text{solarmidnight} + \text{nah} + \text{law} \\
& = \text{sunrise} + \text{law} \\
& = \text{solarnoon} + \text{lah} \\
\end{split}$$ {#eq-sunset}
:::

## Night arc whole {#sec-naw .unnumbered .hiddenheading}

The Sun continues its path after it disappears below the horizon, moving from sunset to sunrise along a "night arc whole" ([naw](#naw){#nightarcwhole .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="night arc"}). Like [conjugate angles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angle#:~:text=conjugate%20angles%20sum%20to%20a%20full%20angle), a [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} and a [naw](#naw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="night arc whole"} form a full circle that represents one day. Likewise, a [lah](#lah){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc half"} and a "night arc half" ([nah](#nah){#nightarchalf .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="night arc half"}) are like two [supplementary angles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angle#:~:text=sum%20to%20a%20straight%20angle) that form a semicircle from solar noon to the [naw](#naw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="night arc whole"} midpoint: [solar midnight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midnight#:~:text=the%20time%20opposite%20to%20solar%20noon%2C%20when%20the%20Sun%20is%20closest%20to%20the%20nadir%2C%20and%20the%20night%20is%20equidistant%20from%20dusk%20and%20dawn).

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup15}
$$\text{naw} = \text{nah} \ast 2$$ {#eq-naw}

$$\begin{split}
\text{day}
& = \text{law} + \text{naw} \\
& = (\text{lah} + \text{nah}) \ast 2
\end{split}$$ {#eq-day}

$$\begin{split}
\text{solarmidnight}
&= \text{sunrise} - \text{nah} \\
&= \text{solarnoon} - \text{lah} - \text{nah} \\
&= \text{sunset} - \text{law} - \text{nah}
\end{split}$$ {#eq-solarmidnight}
:::

The range input below controls the yellow [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} and the blue [naw](#naw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="night arc whole"} in the diagram beneath it. At the Equator, the sun always rises about a quarter turn from North and sets around three quarter turns from North, resulting in a [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} of roughly half a day: 75% [-]{.mono} 25% = 50%. If the [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} is zero, a [polar night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_night#:~:text=the%20Sun%20remains%20below%20the%20horizon%20for%20more%20than%2024%C2%A0hours) occurs. A day without a [naw](#naw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="night arc whole"} is called a [polar day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midnight_sun#:~:text=the%20Sun%20remains%20visible%20at%20the%20local%20midnight).

{{< include /dec/time/_dayarcplot.qmd >}}

The numbers in the diagram above are ["solar azimuth angle"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_azimuth_angle#:~:text=horizontal%20angle%20with%20respect%20to%20north) ([saa](#saa){#solarazimuthangle .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"}) [milliturns]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousandths of a turn"} ([mt](#mt){#milliturn .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliturns"}). At solar noon, the [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"} is 0 [mt](#mt){#milliturn .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliturns"} in the [Southern Hemisphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Hemisphere#:~:text=the%20half%20%28hemisphere%29%20of%20Earth%20that%20is%20south%20of%20the%20equator) and 500 [mt](#mt){#milliturn .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliturns"} in the [Northern Hemisphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Hemisphere#:~:text=the%20half%20of%20Earth%20that%20is%20north%20of%20the%20equator). The [radio](https://observablehq.github.io/framework/inputs/radio#:~:text=allows%20the%20user%20to%20choose%20one%20of%20a%20given%20set%20of%20values)📻input above controls whether the midpoint of the [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} is 0 or 500 [mt](#mt){#milliturn .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliturns"}. To measure the [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"} during the [daytime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daytime#:~:text=the%20period%20of%20the%20day%20in%20which%20the%20Sun%20is%20above%20the%20local%20horizon%20in%20a%20given%20location), point a compass🧭at the spot on the horizon below the Sun.

During an [equinox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equinox#:~:text=a%20moment%20in%20time%20when%20the%20Sun%20appears%20directly%20above%20the%20equator) at the Equator, the Sun goes from East to West directly overhead, the [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"} flips like a switch from 0.25 [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"} to 0.75 [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"} at solar noon, the "[solar elevation angle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_zenith_angle#Summary_of_special_angles:~:text=For%20example%2C%20the-,solar,-elevation%20angle%20is)" ([sea](#sea){#solarelevationangle .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"}) peaks at 0.25 [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"}, and [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"} is 0.5 [−]{.mono} sin([saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"}) &times; (0.25 [−]{.mono} [sea](#sea){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"}). To obtain the [sea](#sea){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"}, we can use the height (h) of a vertical rod on a level surface and the length (L) of its shadow: [sea](#sea){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"} = atan2(h, L).

In addition to determining the [sea](#sea){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"}, the  [atan2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atan2#:~:text=function%20atan2%20is-,the%202%2Dargument%20arctangent,-.%20By%20definition%2C) function can also be used to calculate [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"}, as shown in @eq-astjing, where [j](#j){#jing .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} is a latitude measured in turns called [jīng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meridian_arc#Full_meridian_(polar_perimeter):~:text=The%20polar%20Earth%27s%20circumference%20is%20simply%20four%20times%20quarter%20meridian) ([j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"}). In Dec, [inverse trigonometric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_trigonometric_functions#:~:text=obtain%20an%20angle%20from%20any%20of%20the%20angle%27s%20trigonometric%20ratios) functions like [atan2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atan2#:~:text=function%20atan2%20is-,the%202%2Dargument%20arctangent,-.%20By%20definition%2C) yield [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"} as opposed to [rad](#rad){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="radians"}. At the Equator ([j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} = 0), the latitude is zero and @eq-astjing simplifies to [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"} = 0.5 + atan2(-sin([saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"})cos([sea](#sea){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"}), sin([sea](#sea){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"})).

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup16}
$$
\text{ast} = 0.5 + \text{atan2}\!\!\left(
\begin{aligned}
& \text{-sin(saa)cos(sea),} \\
& \text{sin(sea)cos(j) } - \\
& \text{cos(saa)cos(sea)sin(j)}
\end{aligned}
\right)
$$ {#eq-astjing}

$$
\text{ast} =
\begin{cases}
\text{saa} & \text{j} = 0.25 \\
\text{atan2(-sin(saa)cos(sea), sin(sea))} & \text{j} = 0 \\
(1.5 - \text{saa}) \bmod 1 & \text{j} = -0.25
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-extremes}
:::

At the North Pole ([j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} = 0.25), the latitude is 0.25 [j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} and @eq-astjing simplifies to [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"} = [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"}. At the South Pole ([j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} = -0.25), the latitude is -0.25 [j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} and @eq-astjing simplifies to [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"} = 0.5 [−]{.mono} [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"} before solar noon or [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"} = 1.5 [−]{.mono} [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"} after solar noon. In between the Equator and the South or North Pole (-0.25 < [j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} < 0 &or; 0 < [j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} < 0.25), we should use Equation -@eq-ast, -@eq-astjing, or -@eq-astsha.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup17}
$$
\text{ast} = 0.5 + \text{arccos}\!\!\left(\dfrac{\text{sin(sea)} - \text{sin(j)sin(sda)}}{\text{cos(j)cos(sda)}}\right) \ast
\begin{cases}
\text{-}1 & 0 \le \text{saa} < 0.5 \\
1 & 0.5 \le \text{saa} < 1
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-astsha}
:::

Unlike @eq-astjing, @eq-astsha requires a "solar declination angle" ([sda](#sda){#solardeclinationangle .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar declination angle"}). Whereas latitude is the angle from the Equator in the [geographic coordinate system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geographic_coordinate_system#:~:text=a%20spherical%20or%20geodetic%20coordinate%20system%20for%20measuring%20and%20communicating%20positions%20directly%20on%20Earth%20as%20latitude%20and%20longitude), [declination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declination#:~:text=the%20angular%20distance%20from%20the%20celestial%20equator%20on%20the%20celestial%20sphere) is the angle from the [celestial equator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celestial_equator) in the [equatorial coordinate system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equatorial_coordinate_system#:~:text=a%20celestial%20coordinate%20system%20widely%20used%20to%20specify%20the%20positions%20of%20celestial%20objects). For simplicity, we can use @eq-eot for both the [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} and [sda](#sda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar declination angle"}. The line plot below shows [sda](#sda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar declination angles"} over the course of a year.

{{< include /dec/time/_sdaplot.qmd >}}

In the line plot above, [zero crossings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero_crossing#:~:text=a%20point%20where%20the%20sign%20of%20a%20mathematical%20function%20changes) are [equinoxes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equinox#:~:text=a%20moment%20in%20time%20when%20the%20Sun%20appears%20directly%20above%20the%20equator%2C%20rather%20than%20to%20its%20north%20or%20south) and [stationary points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stationary_point#:~:text=a%20point%20on%20the%20graph%20of%20the%20function%20where%20the%20function%27s%20derivative%20is%20zero) are [solstices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solstice#:~:text=the%20time%20when%20the%20Sun%20reaches%20its%20most%20northerly%20or%20southerly%20sun%20path%20relative%20to%20the%20celestial%20equator%20on%20the%20celestial%20sphere). From the northward to the southward equinox, the [sda](#sda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar declination angle"} is positive and every latitude in the Northern Hemisphere has a [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} that is longer than the [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} at the Equator, whereas every latitude in the Southern Hemisphere has a shorter one. This pattern is reversed when the [sda](#sda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar declination angle"} is negative.

The chart below splits the [Socioeconomic Data and Applications Center](https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/centers/sedac-daac) population data into two bars representing the Northern and Southern Hemispheres and then further divides each bar by [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offset. Nearly 7 billion out of a total of almost 8 billion people live in the Northern Hemisphere and thus experience the longest [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} of the year at the [northern solstice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/June_solstice#:~:text=In%20the%20Northern%20Hemisphere%2C%20the%20June%20solstice%20is%20the%20summer%20solstice%20%28the%20day%20with%20the%20longest%20period%20of%20daylight%29%2C%20while%20in%20the%20Southern%20Hemisphere%20it%20is%20the%20winter%20solstice%20%28the%20day%20with%20the%20shortest%20period%20of%20daylight%29).

{{< include /dec/time/_hemipopplot.qmd >}}

The top range input below picks the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} that we will convert into a [toy](#toy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of year"} and then pass to our [sda](#sda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar declination angle"} model. The two range inputs beneath the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} input choose the geographic coordinates needed to find the sunrise and sunset [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="times of day"}. While the sunrise and sunset [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="times of day"} rely on the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} and both geographic coordinates, the [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} depends on the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} and latitude but not on longitude. The default latitude, 118 [mj](#mj){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millijīng"}, is that of Cambridge, Massachusetts. At the Equator, the [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} is about 0.505 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"} all year long, so the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} input changes the [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} only away from the Equator: \${selectedSunset.toFixed(3)} [-]{.mono} \${selectedSunrise.toFixed(3)} = \${parseFloat(daytimeDuration.toFixed(3))}.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: doyinput
//| class: slider
viewof doyInput = Inputs.range([0, 365], {label: "Day of year", value: 183, step: 1})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: latinput
//| class: slider
viewof latInput = Inputs.range([-250, 250], {label: "Latitude", value: 118, step: 1})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: loninput1
//| class: slider
Inputs.bind(Inputs.range([0, 1000], {step: 1, label: "Longitude"}), viewof lonInput)
```

The equation above can be summarized as sunset [-]{.mono} sunrise = [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} or [minuend](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/minuend#:~:text=A%20number%20or%20quantity%20from%20which%20another%20is%20to%20be%20subtracted) [-]{.mono} [subtrahend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtraction#:~:text=number%20being%20subtracted) = [difference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtraction#Notation_and_terminology:~:text=The%20result%20is%20the%20difference). If we replace the minuend (sunset [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}) with the current [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} and the subtrahend (sunrise [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}) with the sunset [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}, the difference will no longer be the [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} but rather the time until sunset if it is negative or since sunset if it is positive: \${selectedCurrent.toFixed(3)} = \${selectedSunset.toFixed(3)} [${selectedDifference < 0 ? "-" : "+"}]{.mono} \${parseFloat(Math.abs(selectedDifference).toFixed(3))}.

In general, the subtrahend is the time of an event such as a rocket🚀launch and the difference is the negative [remaining time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countdown#:~:text=the%20time%20remaining%20before%20an%20event) if the minuend is less than the subtrahend or the positive [elapsed time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission_Elapsed_Time) if the minuend is greater than the subtrahend. When the minuend is the current time, the difference acts as a ["T minus (T[-]{.mono}) countdown"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countdown#:~:text=a%20sequence%20of%20backward%20counting%20to%20indicate%20the%20time%20remaining) or ["T plus (T+) countup"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countdown#:~:text=After%20a%20launch%2C%20most%20countdown%20clocks%20begin%20to%20show%20Mission%20Elapsed%20Time).

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup18}
$$\begin{cases}\text{difference}<0&{\text{if } \text{minuend} < \text{subtrahend};}\\\text{difference}=0&{\text{if minuend} = \text{subtrahend};}\\\text{difference}>0&{\text{if minuend}>\text{subtrahend.}}\end{cases}$$ {#eq-difference}
:::

Dec uses the term "minuend expansion" to describe the replacement of a minuend with a subtrahend and a difference. We can replace the current [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} with the sum of either zero and a "positive interval [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}" ([pit](#pit){#positiveintervaltod .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive interval tod"}), which is the time since the start of the current day (the previous midnight), or 1 day ([d](#d){#day .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}) and a "negative interval [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}" ([nit](#nit){#negativeintervaltod .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative interval tod"}), which is the negative of the time until the start of the next day (the next midnight), as shown in @eq-todexpansion below. At [Tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} [7]{.color7}, the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} and [pit](#pit){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive interval tod"} are both 0.7 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"} and the [nit](#nit){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative interval tod"} is -0.3 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"}: 0.7 = 0 + 0.7 = 1 + (-0.3).

Likewise, a "positive interval [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"}" ([pia](#pia){#positiveintervalada .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive interval ada"}) is the time since the start of the current year and a "negative interval [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"}" ([nia](#nia){#negativeintervalada .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative interval ada"}) is the time until the start of the next year. A [pia](#pia){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive interval ada"} equals the current [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"}, and a [nia](#nia){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative interval ada"} is the [pia](#pia){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive interval ada"} minus the [syl](#syl){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar year length"}, just as a "negative integer [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"}" ([nid](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"}) is a "positive integer [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"}" ([pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"}) minus the [syl](#syl){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar year length"}. @eq-adaexpansion applies minuend expansion to the [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"}.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup19}
$$\text{tod} = 0 + \text{pit} = 1 + \text{nit}$$ {#eq-todexpansion}

$$\text{ada} = 0 + \text{pia} = \text{syl} + \text{nia}$$ {#eq-adaexpansion}
:::

Declock measures time in fractional days. A single decimal [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} replaces the three parts of an [hms](#hms){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour minute second"} triplet and can be shown at any precision by changing its metric prefix. With one [b9](#b9){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base9"} digit and one [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} digit after four [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"} digits, a [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} can match any [hms](#hms){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour minute second"} triplet exactly, and a [uto](#uto){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="universal time offset"} keeps Dec in step with [ut](#ut){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Universal Time"} without leap seconds. Dec derives its ten [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offsets"} from longitude and never uses negative offsets, but it lets anyone write any [sto](#sto){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar time offset"} after a [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} without forcing them to change it. With the [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} and [sda](#sda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar declination angle"}, we can turn a Zone [0]{.color0} [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} into solar time and estimate the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="times of day"} of sunrise, solar noon, and sunset. Finally, minuend expansion turns any [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} into a countdown or countup relative to an event, such as midnight, sunset, or the start of the year.

# Next {#next .unnumbered}

The next article in the [Dec section](/dec) of my [site](/) shows how we can combine [Dec dates](/dec/date) and times into [Dec snaps](/dec/snap)🫰, which are analogous to the [combined date and time representations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_8601#Combined_date_and_time_representations) in the [ISO 8601](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_8601#:~:text=an%20international%20standard%20covering%20the%20worldwide%20exchange%20and%20communication%20of%20date%20and%20time%2Drelated%20data) international standard for dates and times. The final article in the Dec section demonstrates how Dec dates, times, and snaps🫰can be paired up to express [time intervals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_8601#Time_intervals:~:text=the%20intervening%20time%20between%20two%20time%20points) called Dec [spans](/dec/span)🌈.
